figures.caption: Figure 6: Grad-CAM heatmaps on a forged frame. Xception focuses broadly on central facial regions, while SPSL and LBP highlight phase and texture inconsistencies near the jaw and lips. WDF emphasizes boundary and hairline areas where low-frequency blending artifacts often occur. Fusion-based models (LFWS, LFWL) yield more comprehensive attention across discriminative regions.

Table 1: Forgery detection AUC trained on FF++ (c23). Top-3 average AUC values are highlighted in deep blue. The bottom row reports the relative change (%) in average AUC over the Xception baseline, illustrating the benefit of integrating handcrafted and fused features for cross-domain robustness.

Table 3: AUC comparison across alternative backbones. Baseline backbones without additional features are included for reference. The bottom two rows summarize the average AUC across all datasets and the relative change (%) over each backbone’s baseline, demonstrating the added value of incorporating handcrafted features through the (frozen) fusion block.

Figure 1: Comparison of the two feature integration strategies. Method 1 naively concatenates a handcrafted feature map with RGB inputs, while Method 2 fuses selected feature maps into a compact representation, improving both accuracy and efficiency.

Table 2: Forgery detection AUC trained on DFDCP. Top-3 average AUC values are highlighted in deep blue. The bottom row reports the relative change (%) in average AUC over the Xception baseline, illustrating the benefit of integrating handcrafted and fused features for cross-domain robustness.
Figure 4: Frozen Fusion Block Inference Setup. The fusion block (trained with Xception on FF++) is frozen and reused as a preprocessing step for other backbones.
